items.prompt: What is exposure?
choices: Being able to use the information with the source closed
Explaining the whole topic to a complete beginner from memory alone
Encountering information by reading, hearing or watching it
items.explanation: Exposure is contact with the material, with nothing tested.

items.prompt: Which of these is understanding?
choices: Saying 7×8 is 56 with no sheet in front of you
Reading the 7×8 row one more time again
Highlighting the 7×8 row in bright yellow
items.explanation: Understanding means producing it unaided.

items.prompt: Watching ten cooking shows is mainly which of these?
choices: Proof of cooking skill
Exposure to cooking
A cold test of a recipe
items.explanation: Watching is contact. Cooking the dish is the use.

items.prompt: Priya read her table five times. That was...
choices: Understanding, because it was repeated
Exposure, because nothing tested her
A cold quiz of her memory
items.explanation: Repeating a read is still only contact.

items.prompt: Why do exposure and understanding get confused?
choices: Both take exactly the same amount of time
Both are tested by the same kind of quiz
Both leave a feeling of knowing it
items.explanation: The shared feeling of familiarity hides the difference.

items.prompt: Which sentence shows understanding?
choices: I can explain it without looking at the page
I have read it a great many times already
It looks very familiar to me now, so I must know it
items.explanation: Explaining unaided is use; familiarity is not.

items.prompt: Highlighting a page of notes is...
choices: Exposure, since it tests nothing
Understanding, since you picked the key lines
A cold retrieval test of the page
items.explanation: Highlighting is a passive way to meet the page again.

items.prompt: What does being able to use something mean?
choices: Having met it many times before
Applying it to a new case with no help
Feeling comfortable when you see it
items.explanation: Use means no help and a case you have to handle.

items.prompt: A friend has watched three tutorials and says 'I understand it now.' What is the gap in that claim?
choices: Three tutorials is too few a number, and a larger count of tutorials would settle it
Watching is exposure; nothing shows they can apply it unaided
Tutorials can never teach anything, since only reading printed books builds real skill
Understanding only ever happens when a teacher is physically present in the room
items.explanation: Watching never tested whether it can be applied. The number of tutorials is beside the point.
items.reference:
Two different activities
📖 Exposure: reading, hearing or watching it
🛠️ Understanding: using it with the source closed
🍳 Ten cooking shows are exposure; cooking the dish is use
Why: meeting information and being able to use it are different skills that feel alike.
items.learnMore:
Exposure is contact; understanding is use

These are not a small amount and a large amount of the same thing. Priya's five rereads were contact, and the cold quiz was the first test of use.

Common mistake

Treating lots of exposure as a smaller amount of understanding, rather than a different activity.
items.reflection: Think of something you have watched or read a lot about but never done. What would a cold test of it look like?

items.prompt: A child watches twenty swimming videos, then cannot float at the pool. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The videos were poor quality, and better ones would transfer
Twenty is too few, and thirty videos would be enough
Swimming cannot be learned except from a teacher
The videos gave exposure, and staying afloat is a skill never practiced
items.explanation: Contact with a skill is not use of it, however many videos.

Reading a recipe ten times versus reading it twenty times
Reading one recipe versus reading a whole cookbook
A short recipe read once versus a long one read once
items.explanation: Only the first pair swaps reading for using. The others vary how much was read.

choices: Priya is weak at maths and should probably stop studying the table
Rereading lowered her score from Monday's 90%
Five rereads did not make nine of the questions retrievable

items.explanation: The score shows what was retrievable. Monday's 90% was a feeling, so nothing fell from it.

items.prompt: What is the fluency illusion?
choices: Forgetting what you read soon after
Reading so fast that nothing sinks in at all
Mistaking easy to read for able to produce
items.explanation: The page feels easy, and the feeling is taken for skill.

items.prompt: Why did the fifth read feel smoother than the first?
choices: The page had become easier to process
Priya's memory had become perfect
The table itself had become simpler
items.explanation: Familiar material is processed faster.

items.prompt: Which usually feels easier but tests less?
choices: A cold quiz
Rereading
Both feel the same
items.explanation: Rereading is low effort and checks nothing.

items.prompt: A smooth read tells you mostly that...
choices: You can produce it unaided on demand
You will still remember it next month
The page is easy for you to process
items.explanation: Smoothness is about the page, not about your memory.

items.prompt: Which of these is an active recall move?
choices: Read the chapter a second time
Highlight the main points in a color
Close the book and write what you remember
items.explanation: Active recall means producing, with the source closed.

items.prompt: After reading a chapter, what is a good next step?
choices: Close it and try to reproduce the key points
Move straight on to the next chapter of the book
Read the same chapter once more from the top
items.explanation: A retrieval step turns reading into a test.

items.prompt: Priya felt 90% ready. That number came from...
choices: A quiz she had already passed
How smooth the reading felt
Her dad's cold questions
items.explanation: No one had tested her yet, so it was a feeling.

items.prompt: Does the fluency illusion mean reading is pointless?
choices: Yes, because reading never helps anyone at all
No, it warns against stopping at the reading
Yes, because reading only works a single time
items.explanation: Priya had to read the table first. The error is stopping there.

items.prompt: Which situation shows the fluency illusion at work?
choices: A student forgets most of her notes within days of finishing the exam
A student feels very nervous in the exam room and goes blank on easy items
A student skips the notes entirely and trusts her gut instinct instead
A student rereads notes and feels surer each time, but is never tested
items.explanation: The rising confidence comes from ease of reading with no test behind it.
items.reference:
Why the fifth read feels best
📖 Read 1: slow, every row is new
📖 Read 5: smooth, the page is easy to process
🎯 Cold quiz: the page is gone, and only memory is left
Why: ease of reading grows with every pass, but ability to produce does not have to.
items.learnMore:
Smooth is not the same as known

Each reread makes the page easier to process. That ease is real, and it gets misread as skill. A cold attempt is the check that cannot be fooled this way.

Common mistake

Treating the feeling of clarity as the result of learning, instead of a feeling about the page.
items.reflection: When did you last feel sure about something, then find you could not do it? What had you been doing to prepare?

items.prompt: What does the 50-point gap between Monday's 90% and Wednesday's 40% compare?
choices: A lie Priya told with a true score
A feeling from reading with a result from retrieval
An unfair quiz with an easier Friday quiz
Her memory on Monday with her memory on Wednesday
items.explanation: Nothing tested retrieval on Monday, so the two numbers are different kinds of thing.

Neither, as both studied the same page
B's, because her check produced a result rather than a feeling
A's, because rereading is the harder and more effortful of the two methods

items.prompt: Recognition means...
choices: Pulling it from memory with nothing shown
Having seen something once before
Picking the right thing when it is shown
items.explanation: Recognition needs the answer to be in front of you.

items.prompt: Retrieval means...
choices: Pulling it from memory with nothing shown
Spotting the right option on a list
Reading it more smoothly than before
items.explanation: Retrieval has no prompt except the question.

items.prompt: Which of these is retrieval?
choices: Saying 56 for 7×8 with no page
Seeing 56 and thinking it looks right
Reading the 7×8 row aloud
items.explanation: Producing it from nothing is retrieval.

items.prompt: A multiple-choice question mostly tests...
choices: Retrieval
Recognition
Neither one
items.explanation: The right answer is on the page, so you only have to spot it.

items.prompt: Which loop ends on a feeling?
choices: The active loop itself
Both of the loops
The passive loop
items.explanation: The passive loop stops at 'that felt smooth'.

items.prompt: The key step of the active loop is...
choices: Closing the source and reproducing it
Reading it one more time, a bit slower
Highlighting the parts that look weak
items.explanation: Closing the source is what makes it a test.

items.prompt: In the active loop, finding a gap means...
choices: Stop; the loop has failed
Go back, restudy it, then try again
Move on, because a gap is perfectly normal
items.explanation: The gap is the output the loop exists to find.

items.prompt: Perceptual fluency is...
choices: Speaking a new language smoothly in conversation
Producing an answer without any help at all
Feeling a page is easy because you have seen it
items.explanation: It is ease of processing, not ability to produce.

items.prompt: A fan of a cooking show can pick the right recipe from a list of four, but cannot cook it. Which skill did the list test?
choices: Retrieval, because choosing from a list matched what a real kitchen demands
Recognition, while cooking needs retrieval of steps and amounts
Understanding, so her failure in the kitchen is a complete surprise
Perceptual fluency only, with recognition playing no part in picking from it
items.explanation: A list shows the answer. A kitchen does not.
items.reference:
Two ways to know 56
👀 Recognition: see 56 beside 7×8 and think 'yes'
🧠 Retrieval: say 56 with the page blank
🔁 Passive loop ends on a feeling; active loop ends on a result
Why: recognition needs the answer shown, retrieval does not, and real tasks usually do not show it.
items.learnMore:
Recognition is weaker than retrieval

Picking the right option from a list needs far less than producing it from nothing. Rereading trains the first and a cold attempt tests the second.

Common mistake

Assuming that being able to spot the right answer means being able to give it.
items.reflection: Where in your life do you only ever recognize things, such as a song or a route, and never produce them?

items.prompt: In the Feynman technique you explain the idea to...
choices: An expert, using precise technical jargon
Nobody, by rereading
An imagined beginner, in plain words
items.explanation: Plain words leave nowhere for jargon to hide.

items.prompt: While you explain, the source should be...
choices: Closed
Open beside you
Open only for the hard parts
items.explanation: Closing it is what makes the explanation a test.

items.prompt: A stall is...
choices: A step you explained a little too slowly for the listener
A point where you fall back on 'it just works'
A mistake in the source text that you spotted
items.explanation: A stall marks where retrieval ran out.

items.prompt: Jargon as a placeholder is...
choices: A term that is spelled correctly on the page
A term used without saying what it does
A short word used in place of a long one
items.explanation: Naming a thing is not explaining it.

items.prompt: What do you do with a spot where you stalled?
choices: Reread the entire chapter from the start
Skip it, since you got the rest
Restudy that spot, then explain again
items.explanation: The stall tells you exactly where to go.

items.prompt: What is the main value of the technique?
choices: Each break marks exactly what to study next
It makes the material shorter to read
It removes the need for any studying
items.explanation: It is a diagnostic, not a shortcut.

items.prompt: How much should one round of the technique cover?
choices: A single idea
The whole chapter
Every chapter in the book
items.explanation: A narrow target makes the gaps visible.

items.prompt: Why explain it to a beginner?
choices: Beginners are easier to impress with big words
Plain words leave nowhere for jargon to hide
It takes less time than telling an expert
items.explanation: A beginner needs the mechanism, so a hollow term shows up.

items.prompt: Someone explaining how a bicycle stays upright says: 'it uses angular momentum, which keeps it stable.' Which tell is this?
choices: A stall, because they stopped speaking in the middle of a sentence
Neither, because naming the physics shows that they understand it well
A factual error about how a bicycle stays upright while it moves
Jargon as a placeholder: the term is named but never explained
items.explanation: The term sits where the mechanism should be.
items.reference:
The Feynman loop
1. Pick one idea
2. Explain it in plain words, source closed
3. Mark every stall and unexplained term
4. Restudy only those spots, then explain again
Why: each break in the explanation is a precise pointer to what to study next.
items.learnMore:
The breaks are the diagnostic

Explaining is not the goal. The goal is the list of places where the explanation stalls or leans on a word it never defined, because that list is the study plan.

Common mistake

Rereading the whole source after a stall instead of only the spot that stalled.
items.reflection: Pick something you do every day. Could you explain how it works to a beginner without using any of its jargon?

items.prompt: After finding three stalls in her explanation, what should she do next?
choices: Reread the full source twice, then move to the next idea
Restudy those three spots only, then explain the whole idea again
Explain just those three spots to a friend and stop
Write a summary of the source and keep it nearby
items.explanation: The stalls are the study plan, and a second explanation checks the repair.

choices: A more confident feeling about it
A shorter table to learn
A real score based on retrieval
items.explanation: It was the first number not based on how the page felt.

items.prompt: Priya got 6 of 15 right. What percent is that?
items.explanation: 6 divided by 15 is 0.40.

items.prompt: Where did most of her misses fall?
choices: On 7×1 through 7×5
From 7×6 upward
Evenly across every row
items.explanation: The misses clustered in the later rows.

items.prompt: How many flashcard sessions did she run?
choices: One single long one
Five full ones
Three short ones
items.explanation: Three sessions of about ten minutes each.

items.prompt: What did her flashcards cover?
choices: The whole table, spread out evenly
Only the six she already got right
Only the nine missed questions
items.explanation: The cards were aimed at the gaps.

items.prompt: Why say the answer aloud before flipping?
choices: It forces a retrieval attempt first
It makes the cards look neat and tidy
It lets her skip the wrong ones
items.explanation: Saying it first is the test.

items.prompt: On Friday she scored 14 of 15. What did she miss?
choices: 7×1, once
7×12, once
Several of the middle rows
items.explanation: She missed 7×12 once, a gap the plan was aimed at.

items.prompt: Is the discomfort of recall a sign it is not working?
choices: Yes, it ought to feel smooth and easy
No, the effort is part of how it works
Yes, she should stop and reread instead
items.explanation: A slower, harder attempt is what builds the memory.

items.prompt: A cold quiz gives 6 of 15, with misses clustered from 7×6 upward. What is the best plan for the two days left?
choices: Reread the entire table twice over, because every row matters equally here
Drill cards for the nine misses, saying each answer aloud first
Rest until Friday so that the table can settle properly in her memory
Write the table out three times while looking at the printed sheet
items.explanation: The quiz located the gap. Active recall on it is the efficient use of limited time.
items.reference:
Priya's five days
📖 Mon: 5 reads, felt 90%
❓ Wed: 6 of 15 right = 40%, misses mostly from 7×6 up
🔁 Wed night, Thu: 3 recall sessions on the 9 misses
🏁 Fri: 14 of 15 right = 93%
Why: the cold quiz is a map of the gap, and practice aimed at it beats even rereading.
items.learnMore:
Let the misses choose the practice

A cold test does two jobs: it gives an honest score and it shows where the gaps are. Spending the next session on those gaps is worth more than another even pass.

Common mistake

Rereading everything after a test, including the parts the test showed were already solid.
items.reflection: Think of a recent test, review or trial run. Did the errors show a pattern you could have aimed practice at?

items.prompt: Suppose Priya's misses had been scattered evenly with no solid core. What would that suggest?
choices: Targeted recall is still the right step, run with the same nine cards
The quiz was unreliable, so she should simply retest immediately instead
The table cannot really be learned, so she should stop trying to learn it
No solid base yet, so a fuller pass should come before targeted recall
items.explanation: Targeted recall needs known gaps against a solid base.

Let the misses choose the practice

A cold test does two jobs: it gives an honest score and it shows where the gaps are. Spending the next session on those gaps is worth more than another even pass.

Rereading everything after a test, including the parts the test showed were already solid.
